newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Scandinavia celebrates the 1996 Nobel Prize awards.
newsitem.headline: Scandinavia celebrates the 1996 Nobel Prize awards.

text.p: Scandinavia marked the high-point of its social season on Tuesday as the 1996 Nobel prize winners received their awards in formal ceremonies ahead of glittering banquets in Stockholm and Oslo.
In a two-hour ceremony at the Stockholm Concert Hall, five of the six Nobel prizes received their prizes from King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden.

Earlier in Oslo, Nobel Committee chairman Francis Sejersted presented the 1996 Peace Prize to East Timor human rights campaigners, Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and self-exiled activist Jose Ramos Horta.

Belo and Ramos Horta called on Jakarta to open peace talks in the Indonesian-ruled territory, a former Portuguese colony which was invaded in 1975 after the collapse of Portugal's dictatorship a year earlier. Indonesia declared East Timor its 27th province on July 17, 1976.

The presentation of the Nobel prizes, carrying a prize of $1.2 million each this year, is always split between Stockholm and Oslo as stipulated in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards, first presented in 1901.
This year's awards marked the 100th anniversary of the death of Stockholm-born Nobel, a chemist who invented dynamite.

"He demonstrated that his vision was to work for the benefit of humanity. His donation has very much fulfilled its purpose," yjr chairman of the Nobel Foundation board, Professor Bengt Samuelsson, told Sweden's social elite at the ceremony.
The Nobel awards have become widely recognised as the most prestigious in their fields -- and a ticket to the Nobel banquet is one of the most sought after commodities in Sweden.
The winner of this year's literature prize, Polish poet Wislawa Szymborska, joins the exclusive list of laureates that includes Samuel Beckett, T.S. Eliot, and Albert Camus.
The shy, silver-haired 73-year-old was clearly uncomfortable with the hoard of photographers trying to get a shot of her holding her gold Nobel medal.
"Wislawa Szymborska's making of poems is the perfection of the word object, of the exquisitely chiselled thought-image," said writer Birgitta Trotzig, a member of the Swedish Academy.
The presentation of the 1996 economics prize was tinged with sombreness as observers honoured laureate William Vickery who died of a heart attack three days after winning the prize.

Canadian-born Vickery, 82, won the Nobel economics prize jointly with James Mirrlees, 60, of Britain for their separate contributions to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information. His friend and colleague, Professor C. Lowell Harris received the prize on his behalf.

American trio David Lee, born in 1931 and Douglas Osheroff and Robert Richardson, both born in 1937, won the physics prize for their discovery on the superfluidity of the helium-3 isotope, a break-through in low temperature quantum physics.

Three chemists -- American Robert Curl, fellow countryman Richard Smalley, and Briton Sir Harold Kroto -- were recognised for a 1985 discovery of the "buckministerfullerene", a stable form of carbon in which 60 carbon atoms are arranged in a faceted soccer ball shape.
"This year's Nobel Prize in chemistry has implications for all the natural sciences," Professor Lennart Eberson, a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, said.

Australian Peter Doherty, 55, and Swiss Rolf Zinkernagel, 52, shared the medicine prize for discovering how the immune system recognises and can then kill infected cells, unlocking the mystery of how a vaccine needs to be composed.
Following the award ceremony, the Nobel winners were to join 1,300 people at an exclusive, black tie dinner in Stockholm's City Hall.
